summary: Provides a framework for survivability in MPLS-TP networks, covering how traffic delivery recovers after failure or degradation of network resources. This is critical for services under strict service level agreements. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: MPLS-TP networks need to restore traffic when links or nodes fail, especially for services with strict availability agreements. This RFC organizes recovery options and explains how management, OAM, and control-plane functions can coordinate them.

questions: what is the difference between protection and restoration
subtitle: A framework for restoring MPLS-TP traffic after failures through protection, restoration, and coordinated OAM.

tldr.problem: Services with strict service-level agreements need traffic delivery to recover after a network fault or degradation. MPLS-TP must support recovery with or without a distributed control plane.
tldr.mechanism: The framework organizes recovery by scope, grade, topology, and trigger. Management actions, OAM, and control-plane signaling can configure or initiate data-plane recovery for LSPs.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6372 is an Informational framework, not a protocol specification. Detailed pseudowire recovery and ring-protection mechanisms are outside its scope or specified separately.

facts.label: Automated restoration time
facts.value: Hundreds of milliseconds to a few seconds

today: RFC 6372 is an Informational RFC published in September 2011, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a framework for LSP recovery; detailed pseudowire and ring-protection mechanisms are handled separately.

sections.title: Recovery in MPLS-TP
sections.content:
Survivability is the ability to recover traffic delivery after a fault or denial-of-service attack degrades a network resource. Service Level Agreements (SLAs) may require rapid detection and recovery. MPLS-TP is a packet transport technology based on the MPLS data plane, and this framework describes recovery for its Label Switched Paths (LSPs).

The RFC distinguishes protection, which uses pre-allocated resources, from restoration, which allocates resources when needed, usually by rerouting. Recovery is the general term for both. Protection actions generally complete in tens of milliseconds; automated restoration normally takes hundreds of milliseconds to a few seconds and is not guaranteed.

MPLS-TP can operate without a distributed control plane. Recovery can be initiated by management actions or OAM, and the protection switch itself is a data-plane operation. Detailed pseudowire recovery is beyond the document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Protection uses recovery resources prepared in advance; restoration finds and activates resources after a fault. MPLS-TP recovery can work without a distributed control plane, but this framework focuses on LSPs.

sections.title: Recovery Scope and Service Grade
sections.content:
Recovery may cover a span between neighboring nodes, an LSP segment, or an entire end-to-end LSP. An end-to-end path can be link-diverse or node-diverse, but its ingress and egress nodes remain potential single points of failure.

Dedicated protection assigns resources to a protected path. Shared protection lets several services share recovery resources, saving capacity but potentially leaving some paths unprotected during multiple failures. Extra traffic may use idle protection capacity and can be preempted when protection is needed. Restoration reserves no resources in advance, but it can take longer and may fail if resources are unavailable.

After recovery, traffic may revert to the original working path or remain on the recovery path. A Wait-To-Restore timer can delay reversion to avoid repeated switching when a fault is intermittent.
sections.plainLanguage: Recovery can protect one link, a path segment, or an entire path. Faster or more guaranteed recovery uses more reserved resources; sharing or restoration saves capacity but may leave service unrecovered after multiple faults.

sections.title: Protection Mechanisms and Recovery Domains
sections.content:
The RFC describes link-level protection, alternate paths or segments in the MPLS-TP layer, and pre-provisioned protection tunnels. A tunnel can carry protected LSPs around a failed network segment using label stacking. Link-level protection does not protect the nodes at either end of the protected link.

Protection operates within a recovery domain bounded by reference end points. A recovery group contains a working entity and one or more recovery entities. Domains may be nested but must not overlap. Their edges are not protected unless another recovery domain contains them.

Working and protection paths should avoid shared risks such as two links in one fiber or nodes in one building with a shared power supply. Recovery in layered networks needs coordination and may use a configurable hold-off timer so a lower layer can react before the MPLS-TP layer.
sections.plainLanguage: A recovery domain has endpoints that coordinate a working path and its recovery path. Those paths need to avoid shared physical risks, and recovery across network layers needs coordination.

sections.title: Linear and Shared-Mesh Protection
sections.content:
Linear protection works between pairs of points in a mesh and may protect a node, span, segment, or full path. In 1:1 protection, traffic uses a working path while a protection path is idle. In 1:n protection, one protection entity is shared by several working entities. The endpoints coordinate which path is selected.

In 1+1 protection, the source copies traffic to both working and protection paths, and the sink selects between them. Unidirectional 1+1 does not require endpoint coordination, while bidirectional 1+1 does. Point-to-multipoint 1+1 is described for unidirectional paths; other point-to-multipoint mechanisms are for further study.

Shared mesh protection allows paths with different endpoints to share recovery resources. The RFC says this can reduce reserved resources but becomes more complex as the network and number of LSPs grow. Ring protection is discussed as an area with separate mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: With 1:1 protection, one backup path serves one working path; with 1:n, several paths share a backup. With 1+1, traffic is sent on both paths and the receiver selects which copy to use.

sections.title: Fault Detection, OAM and Coordination
sections.content:
The management plane configures recovery domains, working and recovery entities, protection type, timers, and reversion behavior. Operators may issue commands to block protection, force a switch, request a manual switch, or clear a previous switch command.

OAM can detect continuity loss, misconnectivity, and signal degradation; on-demand trace-route and loopback can help locate faults. For protection switching, a Continuity Check and Connectivity Verification message is commonly sent every 3.33 ms; three consecutive missed messages indicate a fault. Protection endpoints must coordinate their state, and the RFC recommends in-band data-plane signaling for 50-ms protection switching.

The control plane can assist with testing, fault localization and reporting, and establishing protection or restoration LSPs. It cannot detect data-plane faults by itself, and mandatory MPLS-TP survivability features must work even if no control plane is deployed.
sections.plainLanguage: Management configures recovery and allows operator commands, while OAM can detect and locate faults. The control plane can help coordinate and establish paths, but recovery must also work without it.

sections.title: Pseudowires, Manageability and Security
sections.content:
A pseudowire may use recovery of the LSP that carries it or recovery mechanisms in the pseudowire layer. LSP recovery protects individual segments of a multi-segment pseudowire but cannot by itself protect against failure of a pseudowire switching point. Detailed pseudowire recovery is left to separate work.

The framework introduces no new security considerations, but a false OAM fault message could trigger an unwanted switch, displace extra traffic, or leave other services unprotected. Management commands need authorization, and any control-plane protocols used for recovery must provide adequate security. Recovery configuration and OAM operations also have manageability requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: A pseudowire can rely on its carrying LSP or use its own recovery, but detailed pseudowire mechanisms are outside this RFC. OAM, operator commands, and control-plane messages need protection so an attacker cannot trigger or block recovery.
